en: To exist in very large numbers; to be plentiful
hook: A-BOUND-less supply: so much that there's no boundary.
story: In June, mangoes abound in Rajshahi. They pile up on every cart, every rooftop, every kitchen table, until your aunt starts giving them to strangers just to make space. When something abounds, you can't escape it; there is simply more of it than anyone needs. On the GRE, if a passage says errors abound in a theory, it means the theory is full of them.

en: Without a clear shape, form, or structure
hook: A-MORPH-ous: 'a' means without, 'morph' means shape. Without shape.
story: Nadia's study plan began as an amorphous cloud: 'study vocab sometime, maybe math too.' It had no days, no targets, no shape. After failing a practice test, she gave it structure: thirty words every morning and one quant section every night. An amorphous plan is like smoke; you can't hold it. Amorphous means lacking a definite form.

en: Very strict or serious; extremely plain, without comfort or decoration
hook: AUSTERE sounds like 'a stair' of bare concrete: no carpet, no decoration, just hard steps.
story: Rafi's grandfather lived an austere life: one wooden chair, one lamp, rice and lentils every day, and not a single decoration on the walls. He woke at five and never wasted a taka. Visitors found the house cold, but he called it peaceful. Austere means severely simple and strict, with every luxury stripped away.

en: To give a false impression of; to hide the truth behind an appearance
bn: ভুল ধারণা দেওয়া; আসল রূপ আড়াল করা
hook: BE-LIE: the appearance tells a LIE about what's underneath.
story: Tanvir walked out of the GRE center smiling and waving at his friends. But the smile belied his panic; he was sure he had bombed the quant section. His calm face told a lie about what he really felt. When an appearance belies something, it hides the truth or contradicts it. His relaxed walk belied a racing heart.

en: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and unpredictably
hook: CAPRICIOUS sounds like a CAPRI goat: it jumps randomly from rock to rock.
story: Dhaka's weather in April is capricious. At noon the sun burns, at three a storm crashes in, and by five the sky is clear as if nothing happened. You carry an umbrella and sunglasses at the same time. A capricious boss is just as bad: praise on Monday, fury on Tuesday, for no reason. Capricious means unpredictable and impulsive.

en: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical; related to the brain
hook: CEREBRAL = cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.
story: Sara loved cerebral movies, the kind where you need a notebook to follow the plot and argue about it for hours afterward. Her brother preferred action films with car chases and explosions. 'Your movies are too cerebral,' he complained. 'They make my brain hurt.' Cerebral describes anything that appeals to the intellect and thinking rather than to feelings or the body.

en: Pleasant and friendly; well suited to one's taste or nature
hook: CON-GENIAL: comes with a GENIAL, friendly feeling.
story: After months of studying alone, Mitu joined a GRE study group. The members were congenial: they shared notes, laughed at bad mnemonics, and brought tea for everyone. The room felt warm and easy, exactly the kind of place where she could focus. A congenial person or place is agreeable and pleasant, and suits you well.

en: Standing out clearly; easy to notice
hook: CON-SPIC-uous: SPIC sounds like 'spec', as in spectacle. Everyone can see it.
story: At the wedding, everyone wore soft pastel colors except Arif, who arrived in a bright orange suit. He was conspicuous from every corner of the hall; even the photographer kept pointing his camera at him. Conspicuous means obvious and eye-catching. If you want to be conspicuous, wear orange to a pastel wedding.

en: Done quickly and without attention to detail
hook: CURSORY: like moving your CURSOR quickly down a page without reading.
story: Ten minutes before the exam, Rafi gave his notes a cursory glance, flicking through fifty pages in two minutes. He didn't actually read anything. Then the first question asked about a formula he had only skimmed. A cursory look is hasty and superficial, like scrolling your cursor down a page without stopping. Cursory reading leads to careless mistakes.

en: Seeming difficult or intimidating enough to discourage you
hook: DAUNTING sounds like 'DON'T even try', which is what the task seems to say.
story: On the first day, the GRE word list looked daunting: more than a thousand words, many of them strange and impossible to pronounce. Nadia almost closed the file. Then she broke it into groups of thirty, and the mountain became a staircase. A daunting task is one that seems so hard it scares you before you even start.

en: To treat or worship someone as a god
bn: দেবতা জ্ঞান করা; দেবত্ব আরোপ করা
hook: DEI-fy: 'dei' means god, as in deity. To make into a god.
story: Some cricket fans deify their favorite players. They hang giant posters, light candles before matches, and refuse to hear a single word of criticism. When a star scores a century, they treat him almost like a god. To deify someone is to worship them as divine, or to admire them far beyond what any human deserves.

en: Intended to teach a lesson, often in a preachy or moralizing way
hook: DIDACTIC: 'DID you get the lesson? ACT on it!' says the preachy teacher.
story: Every children's story Uncle Karim told was didactic. The lazy rabbit always lost, the honest boy always won, and each tale ended with, 'And the lesson is…' The kids rolled their eyes. A didactic book, film, or speech exists mainly to teach or preach a moral. On the GRE, a didactic tone means the author is lecturing the reader.

en: To spread information or ideas widely
hook: DIS-SEMIN-ate: 'semin' is Latin for seed. Scattering seeds in every direction.
story: When the university changed the exam date, the student union disseminated the news within minutes: Facebook posts, WhatsApp groups, notices taped to every wall. By evening, even students in distant villages knew. To disseminate is to spread something widely, the way a farmer scatters seeds across a whole field so they land everywhere.

en: Possible and practical to do
hook: FEASIBLE: is it EASY-ble? If it can be done, it's feasible.
story: Arif wanted to learn all GRE words in one week. His mentor shook her head. 'That's not feasible. But thirty words a day for five weeks? That's feasible.' A feasible plan is one you can actually carry out with the time and resources you have. Before starting any project, ask: is this feasible, or just a dream?

en: To openly disregard a rule, law, or custom
hook: FLOUT the rule, FLAUNT the attitude: breaking it proudly in public.
story: The sign at the exam center said, 'No phones.' One candidate flouted the rule, scrolling openly in the waiting room while the guard watched. He wasn't sneaky about it; he simply didn't care. To flout a rule is to break it boldly and publicly. Don't confuse it with flaunt, which means to show off.

en: Of the same kind; uniform throughout
hook: HOMO = same, GENE = kind. Same kind all through.
story: The cake batter needs to be homogeneous, Nadia's mother insisted, stirring until no lumps of flour remained and every spoonful looked exactly the same. A homogeneous mixture, a homogeneous group, or a homogeneous neighborhood is uniform: all the parts are alike. Its opposite is heterogeneous, which means mixed and varied.

en: Dull and boring because of being routine
hook: HUM-DRUM: the same humming drumbeat, over and over.
story: Wake up, bus, office, spreadsheet, bus, sleep. Every day of Tanvir's job was humdrum, like a drum hitting the same dull beat forever. Studying for the GRE was the first exciting thing he'd done in years because it promised a new life abroad. Humdrum means monotonous and ordinary, lacking any excitement or variety.

en: Lacking flavor; dull and uninteresting
hook: IN-SIPID: when you SIP it, there's no taste IN it.
story: The hostel dal was insipid: watery, no salt, no spice, nothing. Students joked that it tasted like warm rain. Later, Sara used the same word for a boring lecture, one with no jokes, no examples, and no energy. Insipid describes food without flavor, and also people or ideas without spirit.

en: Talking a lot; very talkative
hook: LOQUACIOUS: 'loqu' means speak, as in eloquent. A loquacious person never stops speaking.
story: The rickshaw puller was loquacious. In a ten-minute ride he told Rafi about his village, his daughter's exams, the price of rice, and his opinion on every politician in the country. Rafi didn't say a single word. A loquacious person talks and talks, sometimes charmingly, sometimes exhaustingly.

en: Disliking and distrusting people in general
hook: MIS = hate, ANTHROP = human. Hating humans.
story: Old Mr. Haque lived alone at the end of the lane. He shut his windows when children played, refused every invitation, and muttered that people were selfish and stupid. The neighbors called him misanthropic. A misanthrope dislikes humanity in general. The opposite is a philanthropist, who loves people and gives generously.

en: A wrong or misleading name
hook: MIS-NOMER: a MIStaken NAME (nomen means name).
story: The shop was called 'Super Fast Internet Café,' but loading one page took three minutes. The name was a misnomer. So is 'koala bear,' since a koala is not a bear at all, and 'peanut,' since it isn't a nut. A misnomer is a name that doesn't fit the thing it describes.

en: Failing to take proper care; careless about duty
hook: NEGLIGENT: someone who NEGLECTS their duty.
story: The guard at the factory was negligent. He slept on duty every night, left the gate unlocked, and never checked the fire alarms. When a fire broke out, the inquiry blamed him for negligence. Negligent means failing to give proper care or attention, especially when it is your responsibility.

en: Too eager to please or obey; excessively flattering
hook: OBSEQUIOUS: 'obsessively SEEK to please us'.
story: Whenever the manager walked by, Kamal jumped up: 'Sir, lovely tie, sir! Tea, sir? Your idea was brilliant, sir!' He laughed at every joke before it ended. His coworkers found him obsequious, too eager to please and too ready to flatter. Obsequious behavior is servile and fawning, and usually fake.

en: To calm someone's anger by doing something to please them
hook: PLACATE: give a PLATE of food to calm someone down.
story: Mitu came home three hours late and found her mother furious. She tried to placate her with apologies, a box of her favorite sweets, and a promise to call next time. Slowly, the anger cooled. To placate is to soothe someone who is angry or upset, often by giving them something.

en: A natural tendency to do something, often something bad
hook: PRO-CLIVITY: like a slope (declivity) you naturally slide down.
story: Arif has a proclivity for procrastination. Give him a week for an assignment and he'll start it the night before, every single time. It's not a choice anymore; it's his natural tendency. A proclivity is an inclination, a habitual leaning toward something, often something you'd be better off avoiding.

en: Childishly silly and immature
hook: PUERILE: 'puer' means boy in Latin. Acting like a little boy.
story: In the middle of a serious meeting, two grown men started throwing paper balls at each other and giggling. Their boss called the behavior puerile. Puerile means childish in an annoying way: silly jokes, petty fights, and immaturity from someone who should know better.

en: Extremely idealistic in an unrealistic, impractical way
hook: QUIXOTIC comes from Don QUIXOTE, the knight who attacked windmills, thinking they were giants.
story: Rafi announced he would end Dhaka's traffic jams alone by standing at intersections and politely asking drivers to take turns. His friends admired his heart but called the plan quixotic. The word comes from Don Quixote, a dreamer who attacked windmills, thinking they were giants. Quixotic means noble but hopelessly unrealistic.

en: A person who spends money wastefully
hook: SPEND-THRIFT: spends away all the thrift (savings).
story: Every month, Tanvir's salary arrived, and within a week it was gone: new sneakers, restaurant dinners, gadgets he never used. By the twentieth, he was borrowing money from his sister. She called him a spendthrift. A spendthrift spends recklessly and wastes money. The opposite is a miser, who refuses to spend at all.

en: Habitually silent; saying very little
hook: TACIT-urn: tacit means unspoken. A person who keeps words unspoken.
story: Nadia's new roommate was taciturn. Ask her how her day was, and she'd say 'fine.' Ask about her family, and she'd nod. In a whole week, she spoke maybe twenty words. She wasn't rude, just naturally quiet. Taciturn is the opposite of loquacious: a taciturn person keeps their words to a minimum.

en: Cautious and alert about possible danger or problems
hook: WARY sounds like WORRY: you worry, so you're careful.
story: After being cheated once by a fake job ad, Sara became wary of offers that sounded too good to be true. Now she checks every company, reads every contract twice, and never sends money upfront. A wary person stays on guard. On the GRE, be wary of answer choices that are too extreme.
